hook_en: Be honest—how many people have you judged today before even knowing the full story?
narration_display: Be honest—how many people have you judged today before even knowing the full story? Iranians have a classic proverb for this: "Mosht-e nemooneh kharvar ast." A single handful tells you about the whole donkey-load. Picture an old bazaar grain merchant. He doesn't dump out every sack to check the wheat. He dips in his hand, feels the grain, smells it, and knows right away. Makes sense, right? A small sample often hints at the bigger picture. We do the exact same thing every day—scrolling a profile, shaking a hand, sizing someone up in thirty seconds. Just remember: a handful only tells the truth if you scooped it fairly. Judge quick if you have to, friend, just stay open to looking a little closer.

hook_en: So someone tried to save a drowning scorpion... and got stung for it.
narration_display: So someone tried to save a drowning scorpion... and got stung for it. There's a famous Persian story about a wise man walking by a stream when he spots a scorpion struggling in the water. He reaches down to pull it out—and ouch, it stings him. He tries again, and again it stings. A watching stranger shakes his head and asks, "Why on earth keep saving something that hurts you?" The wise man smiles gently and says, "Stinging is in its nature. Helping is in mine. Why would I drop my own nature just because it follows its own?" Honestly, that answer hits hard. Still, next time? Grab a leaf or a twig. Be kind, friend—and be smart about how you do it.

hook_en: Imagine grabbing real ice in the middle of a blazing July desert—with zero electricity.
narration_display: Imagine grabbing real ice in the middle of a blazing July desert—with zero electricity. Centuries ago, builders in Iran crafted giant mud-brick domes called yakhchals—literally "ice pits." Their walls were super thick and coated in sarooj, a tough ancient mortar that handled heat and moisture like a champ. Underneath sat a deep underground vault that stayed chilly all year long. How did they make the ice? Winter nights froze shallow pools, workers cut the blocks, and packed them inside. Come hot summer days, that ice was still there—for cold drinks and sweet faloodeh. No AC, no power grid—just pure smart design.

proverb_fa: آب که سر بالا بره، قورباغه ابوعطا می‌خونه
proverb_en: Ab ke sar bala barad, ghorbagheh Abu Ata mikhanad
hook_en: Why does the smallest voice suddenly act like a king the second pressure disappears?
narration: Why does the smallest voice suddenly act like a king the second pressure disappears? In Iran, people expose that exact attitude with one sharp line: Ab ke sar bala barad, ghorbagheh Abu Ata mikhanad. When water rises high, even a tiny frog starts singing a classical melody. Look at a quiet stream at dusk. Low water means silence and discipline. The moment fresh water swells the stream, a tiny frog hops onto a stone and croaks like a master. We have all seen someone act big only because conditions got easy. Sudden comfort or a little attention inflates weak confidence fast. Stay grounded—let real action speak long before the spotlight hits.

proverb_fa: قطره قطره جمع گردد وانگهی دریا شود
proverb_en: Ghatreh ghatreh jam gardad van gahi darya shavad
hook_en: One tiny habit looks laughably small on day one—until a year later it owns the room.
narration: One tiny habit looks laughably small on day one—until a year later it owns the room. A timeless Persian verse says: Ghatreh ghatreh jam gardad van gahi darya shavad. Drop by drop it gathers, and in time becomes an ocean. A single grain of wheat in your palm looks like almost nothing. One cold night freezing a shallow pool looks minor. Yet repeated small steps compound into unstoppable momentum. You do not need a dramatic leap today. Show up, keep the pace steady, and let consistency do the heavy lifting.

proverb_en: Nun-o-mast: Bread and Yogurt Are Not Enough Without Kindness
hook_en: In Iran, a simple meal can reveal a whole heart.
narration: In Iran, a simple meal can reveal a whole heart. Bread and yogurt, nun-o-mast, are the humblest foods in an Iranian home. Yet the proverb says a guest who shares them with warmth honors the table more than any feast. Long ago, travelers on the Silk Road knocked on village doors at dusk, hungry and tired. The wise host did not ask about wealth or status. They asked only whether the traveler had eaten. A torn piece of bread, a spoon of yogurt, and a kind smile could heal a weary soul. The lesson travels with the bread: generosity is not measured by what is on the plate, but by the open heart that offers it.

proverb_en: The Caravan Bell of Rey: A Short Story
hook_en: A bell that could not be silenced once saved an entire caravan from the desert.
narration: Long ago, a merchant named Behrouz led a caravan across the salt desert near Rey. He carried silk, saffron, and a secret he had sworn never to share. One night, a sandstorm swallowed the stars. The camels grew frightened, and the travelers began to scatter. Behrouz remembered his grandmother's words: a true path is found by listening, not by shouting. He tied a small brass bell to the lead camel and let it ring steadily. Each chime was a promise that the path still existed. One by one, the lost travelers followed the sound back to the caravan. At dawn, Behrouz opened his bag and revealed the secret: it was never gold, only the bell that his grandmother had carried across the same desert.

proverb_en: Sheikh Ishraq and the Caravanserai of Light
hook_en: A Persian philosopher once argued that you cannot see the world by light alone, you must first become light.
narration: A Persian philosopher once argued that you cannot see the world by light alone, you must first become light. His name was Shihab al-Din Suhrawardi, born in 1154 near Zanjan, in what is now northwestern Iran. Young, brilliant, and fearless, he founded a school he called Ishraq, or Illumination. Instead of treating knowledge as a dry list of rules, he taught that truth is a living radiance that flows from the highest source down into the soul. He wrote his greatest works in a few short years, often in parables set in strange caravanserais and mountain cities. Scholars still study his Book of Radiance. Many believed his ideas threatened the powerful, and in 1191, at only thirty-eight, he died in prison in Aleppo. Yet his light never went out.
